title: Vector
notes: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. A scalar quantity has only magnitude. Examples: mass, time, temperature, speed, work.

Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction. Negative vector: same magnitude, opposite direction. Null vector: zero magnitude (its direction is undefined). Unit vector: a vector of magnitude 1 along a given direction, written as $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$. Parallel and antiparallel vectors: vectors along the same line (same or opposite sense). Position vector: vector joining the origin to a point. Collinear vectors: vectors along the same straight line.

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$. The result is a scalar. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are perpendicular. For unit vectors: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = 0$.

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta$, directed perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors (right-hand rule). $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are parallel. The cross product is used for torque ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$) and angular momentum ($\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$).
